articles.title: Arizona’s lifeline for chip manufacturing is drying up
articles.summary: America’s epicenter for chip manufacturing has to figure out how to cope with far less water from the Colorado River.
articles.body: Arizona, an epicenter for the bipartisan push to revive American chip manufacturing, is about to lose more than a quarter of the water it typically pulls each year from the Colorado River. The 1,400-mile waterway is a crucial lifeline for the region and other western states. A recent federal decision on how to manage its dwindling flow hits Arizona, and its already drought-prone desert communities, particularly hard. The river provides more than a third of the Grand Canyon State’s water. Arizona has been a manufacturing hub since the start of the semiconductor industry, and now it’s where TSMC and Intel are expanding massive factories to make advanced chips for AI — a water-intensive effort. City planners and industry leaders have already taken precautions to conserve water and find alternative sources. It’s a resource that is likely to become more expensive for manufacturers and residents alike as they learn to rely less on the Colorado River. That’s already raising tensions over who shoulders the costs for new infrastructure needed to adapt, as well as what constitutes a good use of water. The challenges that come with managing a limited water supply are only going to grow as AI demands a larger share. “Our economy is changing, and that’s really painful,” says Kathryn Sorensen, research director at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University. “When there’s a water scarcity issue you have to start looking at what the uses of that water are that bring the most value to the community.” Agriculture has been a major part of Arizona’s economy since it became a state, and still gobbles up more than 70 percent of the state’s water. Industrial uses, including the chip manufacturing that’s had a foothold in the state since the 1940s, account for just 6 percent. While the amount of water that semiconductor factories, or fabs, use is still quite small compared to agriculture, the chip industry is growing fast. Fabs use “ultra-pure” water to clean surfaces and etch sensitive chips. It takes more municipal water to create a smaller amount of ultra-pure water through deionization and reverse osmosis. A typical facility might use 10 million gallons of ultra-pure water a day, which could require up to 16 million gallons of municipal water. New chip factories are sprouting up in Arizona’s desert with the help of federal funding. President Joe Biden signed the ​​CHIPS and Science Act into law in 2022, setting aside $52.7 billion to expand domestic chip manufacturing. Armed with a $7.86 billion grant from the government, Intel is planning to spend $32 billion on two new factories and an expansion of an existing facility in Arizona. In 2025, the company’s facilities in Chandler, Arizona withdrew more than 2.7 billion gallons of freshwater, according to its latest corporate responsibility report. TSMC, the world’s largest chipmaker, received up to $6.6 billion in CHIPS Act funding and decided to build at least six new semiconductor fabs in Phoenix. TSMC’s first fab in Arizona uses roughly 4.75 million gallons of water a day, the company told The Verge last year. It’s approximately equivalent to the water usage of more than 14,000 homes a day, or 2 percent of Phoenix’s housing. That amount grows with each new fab the company builds, and with the more advanced manufacturing processes TSMC is developing. The company recycles 65 percent of the water it uses in Arizona, TSMC says, a figure that’s supposed to grow to at least 90 percent when it finishes building a water reclamation plant. The Colorado River is the state’s biggest renewable source of water. But the Colorado River Basin has faced “unprecedented” drought for more than a quarter century, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation. Climate change, unfortunately, is also making the region more dry as growing water demand adds to decades of overuse. “There’s not enough water for everything we want to do with it,” Sorensen, who previously worked as the director of Phoenix Water Services, says. “So what do we have enough water for? What are the uses we most value? Is it cotton or is it microchips?” With 40 million Americans from Denver to Los Angeles relying on water from the Colorado River, states have been tussling over how to allocate the remaining water for years. Guidelines for how to manage that water, collectively known as the “Law of the River,” expire this year. After states failed to reach an agreement on their own, the US Department of the Interior finalized its own plan in August for how to move forward. It outlines steep cuts for downriver states: Arizona, Nevada, and California. Arizona stands to lose the most, at least 760,000 acre-feet of water a year starting in 2027. An acre-foot represents how much water it would take to cover an acre with a foot of water, and is enough to supply about three homes with water for a year in the Phoenix area. The City of Phoenix uses about 300,000 acre feet of water in a year. Maricopa County, home to Intel and TSMC’s chip fabs, isn’t as reliant on water from the Colorado River as other counties. Its primary resource is groundwater, but surface water flowing from the Colorado and Salt rivers still make up close to 40 percent of the county’s supply. Local leaders insist that Phoenix and other cities in the region are prepared for water cuts, citing plans to make up for the shortfall with underground water stores and other surface water sources. “For the most part, they’ve planned accordingly and can fall back onto water that was previously stored underground,” Sorensen says. But even without sudden tap water shortages, Sorensen expects utility bills to climb over time. The transition to alternative water resources will entail new infrastructure, like new wells and pipes. That’s likely to be the most significant driver of higher tap water prices, Sorensen explains. Meanwhile, the city of Phoenix is pushing back, with Mayor Kate Gallego arguing that the federal government’s decision to cut the state’s intake “does not provide the fair, basin-wide leadership the Colorado River crisis demands.” That said, “Phoenix is prepared for this moment because of decades of planning and conservation, we will push for new federal support to mitigate the rising cost of water that will result from this federal decision,” Gallego added in an August press release. A spokesperson for the city declined to comment further in an interview. TSMC in particular, located in Phoenix, will be subject to the same price hikes as its neighbors. Phoenix is unique in that it sets the same water rates for companies as it does for residential customers. Cities often charge industrial customers less if they want to attract certain businesses. “The cost of water will increase for TSMC,” Sorensen says. “Everyone pays the same rate for water in the city of Phoenix, whether you’re a mom-and-pop store, a family of eight, or TSMC.” TSMC and Intel declined interviews with The Verge for this story. Both have made public commitments, however, to minimize the amount of fresh water they consume. “A stable supply of water is critical to chip production,” TSMC deputy spokesperson Nina Kao said in an emailed statement. “One of the reasons the city of Phoenix was selected for our US expansion is because of their long-term water plan, which includes varied water supply sources, as well as steps taken in preparation for reduced water supplies over the course of decades.” Apprehensions are still mounting over the impact that AI and the tech industry as a whole have on the region. AI has spawned a new generation of semiconductor factories, chip packaging plants, and data centers across Arizona. “It’s almost happening at a level that’s difficult to wrap your head around,” says Jennifer Martin-McLeod, a program manager for the Grand Canyon chapter of Sierra Club. “To try to say ‘Everybody take a breath and think through what we’re doing’ is difficult when you have that steamroller of money coming at your state to try to make it all happen overnight.” She has broader concerns about the health of the Colorado River and wildlife that depends on it. Over the long term, Sorensen points out that a shortage of water from the Colorado River will result in the depletion of groundwater in Central Arizona, as most cities cope by increasing how much water they draw from local aquifers. “It’s something they can sustain, but it is only sustained at a cost to future generations,” she adds. The impact of water cuts next year will be felt most by typical residents, Martin-McLeod says. “For me, that’s going to mean serious lifestyle changes. … But to an enormous chip manufacturer, that’s maybe just part of the cost of doing business, you know?”

articles.title: Scientists fitted GPS collars to 17 lions and 14 hyenas expecting hyenas to follow lions; thousands of locations revealed the opposite, with male lions approaching as hyenas retreated
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Wildlife biologists tracking lions and spotted hyenas in Southern Africa have found evidence that challenges a long-held belief about how the two pred.
articles.body: Wildlife biologists tracking lions and spotted hyenas in Southern Africa have found evidence that challenges a long-held belief about how the two predators interact. Instead of hyenas mainly following lions to find leftover food, the study found that male lions often actively move towards spotted hyenas, while the hyenas try to get away. The study, published in the open-access journal Frontiers in Ethology on September 9, 2026, used thousands of telemetry records to track the movements of the two species in real time. Researchers fitted high-precision GPS collars to 17 African lions (Panthera leo) and 14 spotted hyenas (Crocuta crocuta) living in protected wilderness areas. Researchers had initially expected hyena groups to regularly follow lions, either to take advantage of their kills or to scavenge food left behind. The tracking data showed a different pattern. Male lions often changed direction and moved towards nearby hyenas, while hyenas changed their routes or moved away to avoid potentially dangerous encounters.Tracking data reveals unexpected movement patternsThe international research team used location data collected at regular intervals across several seasons to study the movements of the predators. The large dataset allowed researchers to examine how lions and hyenas responded when they came close to one another, including at night and in areas that were difficult for researchers to observe directly. When male lions came close to spotted hyenas, their GPS tracks often showed a clear change in direction towards the hyenas. This indicated that the lions were not simply encountering their competitors by chance. Instead, they appeared to be actively moving towards them. The behaviour could help lions eliminate competitors or take over kills that hyenas had already secured. Lions and spotted hyenas compete for many of the same prey animals, making encounters between the two species potentially costly for both sides. The hyenas showed the opposite response. Their movement paths generally turned away when lions approached. They appeared to maintain a distance from male lions and changed direction or increased their speed when the predators came too close. "We expected hyenas to track lions to exploit their kills, but the GPS data clearly showed lions taking the initiative," noted the research team in their paper published in Frontiers in Ethology. "Male lions actively moved towards hyena locations, forcing hyenas to take evasive action to avoid dangerous confrontations." The researchers also found differences between male and female lions. Male lions were more likely to move towards hyenas, while lionesses showed more cautious movement. This was particularly noticeable when females were caring for dependent cubs or moving without the protection of a male coalition.The findings challenge the usual predator hierarchyThe results question a common picture of the relationship between lions and spotted hyenas. Spotted hyenas are skilled hunters and can kill large prey without relying on lions. Yet they are often portrayed as scavengers that follow big cats and steal their food. The relationship is more complicated. Lions can also take advantage of kills made by hyenas, particularly because adult male lions have a major physical advantage over individual female hyenas. Male lions can weigh up to twice as much as adult female hyenas. A single male can therefore drive several hyenas away from a carcass or seriously injure one during a confrontation. For hyenas, avoiding a direct fight can be the safer option unless enough members of the clan are present to challenge the lion. The tracking results suggest that this risk shapes where and how hyenas move when lions are nearby. The study therefore points to spatial avoidance as an important survival strategy for spotted hyenas living alongside lions. Hyenas can benefit from searching for food in areas used by lions, but they also have to manage the risk of coming too close to a much stronger predator.GPS collars offer a clearer view of predator behaviourMuch of what scientists previously knew about interactions between lions and hyenas came from observations made during research drives. Those observations can be limited because predators are not always active during daylight hours, while thick vegetation can prevent researchers from seeing encounters. GPS tracking provided a different view. The collars used in the study recorded the animals' locations at regular intervals, allowing researchers to follow their movements across day and night. The technology also made it possible to track animals through areas that researchers could not easily reach. By comparing the movements of lions and hyenas at the same time, scientists could see how one species responded when the other approached. The resulting data offered a more detailed picture of predator interactions than isolated sightings could provide. The research published in Frontiers in Ethology shows how multi-species tracking can help answer questions that have remained difficult to study through traditional field observations.Why the findings matter for wildlife reservesUnderstanding how large predators respond to one another can also help conservation managers plan for wildlife populations in protected areas. Human development has reduced and fragmented many natural habitats, leaving some predator populations increasingly concentrated inside protected reserves. In fenced reserves, lions, hyenas and other large carnivores may have less space to avoid one another or follow natural movement patterns. Knowing how predators respond when they share the same territory can help managers understand where different species are likely to concentrate and how their movements may affect prey populations. The researchers' findings suggest that the relationship between lions and hyenas cannot be described simply as hunters and scavengers. Their movements show a more active contest between two competing predators, with male lions often taking the initiative and spotted hyenas adjusting their behaviour to stay out of danger.

articles.title: Where Did Canada’s Last 6 Captive Belugas Go?
articles.summary: Canada just completed what experts call the largest captive whale relocation in history, and the journey these six belugas took to reach their new homes was...
articles.body:
Canada's last six captive beluga whales were relocated from Marineland to new homes, marking the end of whale or dolphin captivity in the country.

The whales were carefully guided into transport slings, lifted with a crane, and flown to their new homes after the closure of Marineland.

The relocation of the beluga whales was described as the largest ever undertaken, with two going to Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and four to SeaWorld in San Antonio.

Whales are some of nature's most amazing animals. Growing to massive sizes, these animals deserve to spend their time traveling the open seas. Recently, Canada's last captive whales were relocated from the former Marineland to new homes. This Instagram post by @walrus_whisperer shows the parade of vehicles carrying these whales.

On August 31, the final six beluga whales began their removal from the now-shuttered Marineland marine park in Niagara Falls, Canada. This has been described as the largest relocation of captive whales ever undertaken. The whales lived at Marineland, which was once Canada's best-known marine attraction. The park closed to the public in 2024, leaving 30 beluga whales and four bottlenose dolphins behind. As the facility faced growing financial problems and prepared to sell the property, the urgency of finding new homes for the animals increased. Thanks to collaboration between Canadian authorities, veterinarians, and transport crews, the final six whales at the facility were ultimately relocated to new homes.

Two of the whales, Yukon and Gimli, were sent to Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, while Tank, Odin, Orion, and Tofino were sent to SeaWorld in San Antonio. The other beluga whales and dolphins have been distributed to several different facilities in Atlanta, San Diego, and Valencia, Spain. Moving animals of this size requires careful planning. Specialists carefully guided each beluga whale into a transport sling, which was then lifted with a crane.

They were lowered into water-filled transport tanks and then brought to Toronto Pearson International Airport, from where they were flown to their new homes. Traveling is extremely stressful for any animal, but it can be especially difficult for social animals like whales. Because transport can be stressful, veterinarians monitored the whales closely before, during, and after the journey. This move is extremely significant as it marks the end of whale or dolphin captivity in Canada.

articles.title: Lessons from Ukraine war: Poland wants its own Starlink; where does India stand?
articles.summary: News News: Poland is moving to develop its own military satellite communications system in partnership with Finnish space company ICEYE and state-run defence gia.
articles.body: Poland is moving to develop its own military satellite communications system in partnership with Finnish space company ICEYE and state-run defence giant PGZ, in a programme that Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described as a potential “Polish Starlink”.The two companies signed a letter of intent for the project at the MSPO defence show in Kielce on Sept. 9. Tusk said the planned system would be modelled on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network, highlighting the critical role of communications in modern warfare.Under the new partnership, ICEYE will serve as the technology partner, developing the satellite architecture, manufacturing the spacecraft and conducting satellite operations, while PGZ will establish the domestic industrial base and coordinate Polish companies contributing production capabilities, expertise and infrastructure.According to Defense News, PGZ said the programme is planned for implementation between 2026 and 2030. The system is expected to use a distributed satellite architecture, alongside domestic ground infrastructure and industrial capabilities that would allow Poland to independently develop and maintain the system.“Anyone closely following the Russian-Ukrainian war knows how important communications are,” Tusk said, adding that communications are “absolutely critical” on the modern battlefield.Starlink's role in the Ukraine warThe Ukraine war has demonstrated the military value of satellite communications, with SpaceX’s Starlink becoming an important communications network for Ukrainian forces.According to Reuters, Ukrainian military units were heavily reliant on thousands of Starlink terminals for battlefield communications and some drone operations, with the systems proving resistant to espionage and signal jamming.The dependence on Starlink has also exposed the risks of relying on a privately operated system during a war. In July 2025, a global Starlink outage disrupted Ukrainian military communications for about two and a half hours, affecting drone operations and battlefield coordination. A Ukrainian drone commander said several combat operations had to be postponed during the outage.European governments have increasingly looked at reducing their dependence on US satellite communications infrastructure, with the war highlighting both the value of Starlink and the vulnerabilities that can arise from reliance on a single provider.Where India standsIndia has dedicated military satellite communications capabilities for more than a decade. The Indian Navy was the first service to receive a dedicated communications satellite with GSAT-7, launched in 2013. The Indian Air Force later received GSAT-7A, launched in 2018, which provides communication capability to users over the Indian region.A recent assessment by Germany's Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik notes that the GSAT series has increasingly been used to meet India's military communications requirements, with GSAT-7 providing the Navy's sovereign communications infrastructure and GSAT-7A extending such capability to the other armed forces.India has now added a newer and more capable layer to this architecture. CMS-03, also designated GSAT-7R, was launched on November 2, 2025, and was developed specifically for the Indian Navy. The government describes it as India's most advanced communication satellite for the Navy, designed to strengthen space-based communications and maritime domain awareness. The satellite provides coverage across the Indian Ocean Region and weighs about 4,400 kg, making it India's heaviest communication satellite launched from Indian soil.The CMS-03 satellite is intended to support naval communications across a very large maritime area, giving the Navy a dedicated space-based communications layer for operations across the Indian Ocean.
